input.answer:
The sky is blue because of Rayleigh scattering: air molecules are far smaller than the wavelength of visible light, and they scatter short wavelengths much more strongly than long ones. [1]

The effect is steep. Scattered intensity varies with the inverse fourth power of wavelength, so blue light at about 450 nm is scattered roughly 5.9 times more than red light at about 700 nm — a ratio I checked directly rather than taking on trust. Sunlight reaching you from every direction other than the sun itself is therefore dominated by blue. [1]

Two details are worth adding. Violet scatters even more strongly than blue, but sunlight contains less of it and the human eye is less sensitive to it, so the sky reads as blue rather than violet. [1] And at sunset the light travels a much longer path through the atmosphere, by which point most of the blue has been scattered away and the reds and oranges are what remain. [2]
